subject: Chemistry
title: Why the Sky Is Blue
description: A micro-lesson that makes Why the Sky Is Blue usable.

hook.text: Sunlight is white. The atmosphere scatters blue wavelengths more than red—painting the sky blue.

buildup.text: Light from the Sun contains all colors. When it hits nitrogen and oxygen molecules, it scatters.

discovery.text: Short wavelengths (blue, violet) scatter far more than long ones (red, orange). This is Rayleigh scattering.

twist.text: The sky should look violet since violet scatters most. But our eyes are more sensitive to blue than violet.

climax.text: At sunset, light travels through more atmosphere. Blue scatters away, leaving red and orange.

punchline.text: Blue light bounces around the sky. Red punches through at sunset.

quiz.question: Why does the sky appear blue rather than violet?
options: Our eyes are more sensitive to blue than violet light
There is no violet light in sunlight
Violet is absorbed by the ozone layer

details.summary: The sky appears blue because of Rayleigh scattering. Nitrogen and oxygen molecules in the atmosphere scatter shorter blue wavelengths of sunlight much more than longer red wavelengths..
details.whyItMatters: Rayleigh scattering explains not only blue skies but also red sunsets, the appearance of distant mountains, and the design of optical instruments that must account for wavelength-dependent scattering.
takeaways: Short blue wavelengths scatter about ten times more than long red ones
Rayleigh scattering occurs when particles are smaller than light wavelengths
Sunsets appear red because blue light has scattered away over a longer path

faq.question: If violet light has a shorter wavelength than blue, why isn't the sky violet?
faq.answer: The sun emits less violet light than blue light to begin with. Additionally, our eyes are much more sensitive to blue than violet wavelengths. The upper atmosphere also absorbs some violet light. Combined, these factors make the sky appear blue rather than violet to human observers.

faq.question: Why does the sky turn red and orange during sunsets?
faq.answer: At sunset, sunlight travels through much more atmosphere to reach your eyes. The extended path scatters away most blue and green light, leaving primarily red and orange wavelengths to pass through directly. Dust and aerosols enhance the effect by scattering additional wavelengths.
